## Data cleaning

Start by fixing the headers, I make them lowercase and use underscores instead
of spaces.
```{python}
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('data/nypd311w062925noise_by100625.csv')

df.columns = df.columns.str.replace(" ", "_").str.lower()

df.head()
```

In order to get a good view on what data we are missing, I print out the
missing percentage and column name.

With this info we can develop an understanding of how the data should be
cleaned. I immediately remove all of the totally empty columns.

We can also infer that if two columns have the same missing percentage, they
may be missing the same data.

```{python}
missing_percentage = (df.isnull().sum() / len(df)) * 100
print("Percentage of missing values per column:")
print(missing_percentage)

# remove columns that are completely empty
df.dropna(axis=1, how='all', inplace=True)
```

Since `park_borough` and `borough` have the same information, keeping both is
redundant.

I like borough better as a name so I remove `park_borough`.

```{python}
# check if all boroughs are unique 
comparison = df['borough'] == df['park_borough']

# .all() checks if all values in the boolean series are true
are_identical = comparison.all()
print(are_identical)

df.drop('park_borough', axis=1, inplace=True)
```

Here I find that there are some rows contain 'Unspecified' in borough column.

I replace them with NaN for easier comparison later.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# Get the unique items in "borough"
unique_borough = df['borough'].unique()
print(unique_borough)

# Replace the Unspecified items with Na
df['borough'] = df['borough'].replace('Unspecified', np.nan)
```

Status only contains "closed" so drop it.

Agency only contains "NYPD" so drop it.

Unique key is not useful to us, so drop it.

```{python}
# .nunique() counts the number of unique values in the Series
status_is_constant = df['status'].nunique() == 1
print(status_is_constant)

df.drop('status', axis=1, inplace=True)

# We drop duplicates from the two columns to see how many unique pairs exist
df.drop('agency', axis=1, inplace=True)

# 'unique_key' is an identifier, not a feature for analysis, so we drop it.
df.drop('unique_key', axis=1, inplace=True)
```

Only different rows are NaN. So we could remove one column.

```{python}
different_rows_mask = df['cross_street_1'] != df['intersection_street_1']
different_rows = df.loc[different_rows_mask, ['cross_street_1', 'intersection_street_1']]

print(different_rows.head())

# drop this since its the same as intersection street 2
df.drop(columns='cross_street_1', inplace=True)
```

Same thing here, removed cross_street_2 for consistency. 

```{python}
different_rows_mask = df['cross_street_2'] != df['intersection_street_2']
different_rows = df.loc[different_rows_mask, ['cross_street_2', 'intersection_street_2']]

print(different_rows.head())

# drop this since its the same as intersection street 2
df.drop('cross_street_2', axis=1, inplace=True)
```

```{python}
# convert incident_zip to integer first (to remove .0), then to string
# this converts 10001.0 -> 10001 -> '10001'
df['incident_zip'] = pd.to_numeric(df['incident_zip'], errors='coerce').astype('Int64').astype(str)

valid_zip_strings = {str(z) for z in valid_zip}

# Identify invalid zip codes (not in valid set AND not '<NA>')
is_invalid_zip = ~df['incident_zip'].isin(valid_zip_strings) & (df['incident_zip'] != '<NA>')

# Set invalid zip codes to NaN
df.loc[is_invalid_zip, 'incident_zip'] = np.nan

print(f"Valid zip codes remaining: {df['incident_zip'].notna().sum()}")
print(f"Invalid zip codes set to NaN: {is_invalid_zip.sum()}")
print("\nSample valid zip codes:")
print(df['incident_zip'].dropna().head(20))
```

Complaint type has the prefix 'Noise -' before every entry, so I just remove
them to save space.

```{python}
df['complaint_type'] = df['complaint_type'].str.replace('Noise - ', '', regex=False)
```

### Check For date inconsistencies

Here I format the date columns for comparison.

```{python}
# Convert date columns to datetime objects for analysis
df['created_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['created_date'], format='%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p', errors='coerce')
df['closed_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['closed_date'], format='%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p', errors='coerce')
df['resolution_action_updated_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['resolution_action_updated_date'], format='%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p', errors='coerce')
```

Check for complaints where 'closed_date' is before 'created_date'

```{python}
error1_mask = (df['closed_date'].notna()) & (df['closed_date'] < df['created_date'])
error1_count = len(df[error1_mask])

print(error1_count)
```

Check for complaints where 'closed_date' and 'created_date' are identical

```{python}
error2_mask = (df['created_date'].notna()) & (df['closed_date'].notna()) & (df['created_date'] == df['closed_date'])
error2_count = len(df[error2_mask])

print(error2_count)
```

Check if any complaints were created or closed at exactly 12, this would mean
that there is an auto close feature in the system.

```{python}
is_midnight = (df['created_date'].dt.hour == 0) & (df['created_date'].dt.minute == 0) & (df['created_date'].dt.second == 0)
is_noon = (df['created_date'].dt.hour == 12) & (df['created_date'].dt.minute == 0) & (df['created_date'].dt.second == 0)
error3_mask = (df['created_date'].notna()) & (is_midnight | is_noon)
error3_count = len(df[error3_mask])

print(error3_count)
```
Seems like there are no errors in this data from our outputs.

Look at the fully cleaned dataset, I fill in some missing coordinates from the
address column later in this paper.

```{python}
df.head()
```

```{python}
output_path = 'data/nypd311w062925noise_by100625_cleaned.arrow'

# Save the cleaned DataFrame to Arrow format
df.to_feather(output_path)
```

## Data Exploration

Here I'm creating columns in order to do analysis.

We can create the response time column because we know there are no errors. We
can also separate into day or night, there may be an interesting correlation
there. Also weekend vs weekday may show something about the data.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats

df = pd.read_feather('data/nypd311w062925noise_by100625_cleaned.arrow')

# Create response_time column
df['response_time'] = (df['closed_date'] - df['created_date']).dt.total_seconds() / 3600

# Create time_of_day column
df['time_of_day'] = df['created_date'].dt.hour.apply(
    lambda hour: 'Daytime' if 6 <= hour < 20 else 'Nighttime'
)

# Create day_type column
df['day_type'] = df['created_date'].dt.dayofweek.apply(
    lambda day: 'Weekday' if day < 5 else 'Weekend'
)
```

### Time of Day vs Response time

Display descriptive statistics, and create a plot to visualize time vs response
time.

```{python}
time_stats = df.groupby('time_of_day')['response_time'].describe()
time_stats.head()
```

```{python}
df['hour_of_day'] = df['created_date'].dt.hour
df['hour_of_day'] = pd.Categorical(df['hour_of_day'], categories=list(range(24)), ordered=True)

#  Hourly Pattern
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 8))
hourly_avg = df.groupby('hour_of_day')['response_time'].mean()
plt.plot(hourly_avg.index, hourly_avg.values, marker='o')
plt.axvspan(0, 6, alpha=0.2, color='blue', label='Nighttime')
plt.axvspan(20, 24, alpha=0.2, color='blue')
plt.axvspan(6, 20, alpha=0.2, color='yellow', label='Daytime')
plt.title('Average Response Time by Hour of Day')
plt.xlabel('Hour of Day')
plt.ylabel('Average Response Time (Hours)')
plt.xticks(range(24))
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
```
From this visualization we can see that there seems to be a difference between
response time during day and night, in order to confirm this we could perform
a hypothesis test.


H0: Response times do not differ between day and night.

HA: day time response time is different from night time response time.

```{python}
# Separate the data into two groups
daytime_response = df[df['time_of_day'] == 'Daytime']['response_time']
nighttime_response = df[df['time_of_day'] == 'Nighttime']['response_time']

# Perform a t-test
t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(nighttime_response, daytime_response, equal_var=False)

print("\nStatistical Test Results:")
print(f"T-statistic: {t_stat:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
```
According to this our p-value is much smaller than 0.05, we reject H0, and there
is significant statistical evidence that response time differs between day and
night time.

### Complaint type (descriptor) Day and Night vs. response time. 


```{python}
complaint_time_data = df.groupby(['descriptor', 'time_of_day'])['response_time'].mean().unstack()

# Create the grouped bar chart
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 8))
complaint_time_data.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(14, 8), width=0.8)

# Customize the plot
plt.title('Average Response Time by Complaint Type and Time of Day', fontsize=16)
plt.ylabel('Average Response Time (Hours)', fontsize=12)
plt.xlabel('Complaint Type', fontsize=12)
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.legend(title='Time of Day')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
From this visualization we can see that there seems to be a difference between
complaint descriptor response time on average. In order to test this we can set
up an ANOVA test to compare each complaint type to response time.

H0: All descriptor mean response times are equal.

HA: At least one differs.


```{python}
complaint_groups = [group['response_time'].values for name, group in df.groupby('descriptor')]

f_statistic, p_value = stats.f_oneway(*complaint_groups)

print(f"F-statistic: {f_statistic:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
```
We reject H0, the p-value is much smaller than 0.05. 

It is evident that there is a statistically significant difference in mean
response time per descriptor.

### Response Time Vs Borough (day and night).

```{python}
borough_time_data = df.groupby(['borough', 'time_of_day'])['response_time'].mean().unstack()

plt.figure(figsize=(14, 8))
borough_time_data.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(14, 8), width=0.8)

plt.title('Average Response Time by Borough Type and Time of Day', fontsize=16)
plt.ylabel('Average Response Time (Hours)', fontsize=12)
plt.xlabel('Borough', fontsize=12)
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.legend(title='Time of Day')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

This chart shows that there is definitely some variance between boroughs and
response times.

It seems the slowest is Bronx during the day.

We can test our hypothesis that there is a difference between mean response time
per borough. We can use a one way ANOVA test.

H0: Mean response time per borough does not differ.

HA: At least one borough differs in mean response time.

```{python}
borough_groups = [group['response_time'].values for name, group in df.groupby('borough')]

# --- Step 3: Perform the One-Way ANOVA Test ---
f_statistic, p_value = stats.f_oneway(*borough_groups)

print(f"F-statistic: {f_statistic:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
```

Since our p-value is much smaller than 0.05, we can reject H0. There is
significant statistical evidence to conclude that there is a difference between
mean response time per borough.

### Mean response time vs type of day (weekday or weekend)

```{python}
df['day_type'] = df['created_date'].dt.dayofweek.apply(
    lambda day: 'Weekday' if day < 5 else 'Weekend'
)

day_time_data = df.groupby(['day_type', 'time_of_day'])['response_time'].mean().unstack()

# 2. Create the grouped bar chart
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
day_time_data.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(10, 7), width=0.8)

# 3. Customize the plot
plt.title('Average Response Time by Day Type and Time of Day', fontsize=16)
plt.ylabel('Average Response Time (Hours)', fontsize=12)
plt.xlabel('Day Type', fontsize=12)
plt.xticks(rotation=0) # Keep the x-axis labels horizontal for clarity
plt.legend(title='Time of Day')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
From this chart we can see that there does not seem to be a large difference
between response times on weekends and weekdays. We can use a T-test to test
our hypothesis.

H0: There is no difference between mean response times between day types.

HA: Mean response time differs between day type.

```{python}
day_groups = [group['response_time'].values for name, group in df.groupby('day_type')]

f_statistic, p_value = stats.f_oneway(*day_groups)

print(f"F-statistic: {f_statistic:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
```
There is insufficient evidence to conclude there is a difference in response
times on weekends compared to weekdays.

### Testing Correlations
In this subsection we test to see if there is a correlation between some
variables and a new variable `over2h`, which is declared below.

```{python}
df['over2h'] = df['response_time'] >= 2
```
Since this is a binary variable, we can test correlation using chi squared tests.

#### Time of day vs Over 2 Hrs.

```{python}
contingency_table = pd.crosstab(df['time_of_day'], df['over2h'])
chi2, p_value, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(contingency_table)

print(contingency_table)

print(f"Chi-square statistic: {chi2:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
```
Since our p-value is much smaller than 0.05. There is statistically significant
evidence to show that over 2 hrs depends on time of day.

#### Day Type vs Over 2 Hrs.

```{python}
df['is_weekend'] = df['created_date'].dt.dayofweek >= 5

contingency_table = pd.crosstab(df['is_weekend'], df['over2h'])

print(contingency_table)
```

```{python}
chi2, p_value, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(contingency_table)
print(f"Chi-square statistic: {chi2:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
print(f"Degrees of freedom: {dof}")
```

The result is statistically significant. There is a strong association between
whether a complaint is made on a weekend and whether it takes over 2 hours to
resolve.

```{python}
contingency_table = pd.crosstab(df['descriptor'], df['over2h'])

print("Contingency Table (Complaint Type vs. Over 2 Hours):")
print(contingency_table)

chi2, p_value, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(contingency_table)

print("Chi-Square Test Results for Complaint Type vs. Over 2 Hours:")
print(f"Chi-square statistic: {chi2:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
print(f"Degrees of freedom: {dof}")
```
There is a statistically significant association between complaint type and
whether a request takes over 2 hours.

```{python}
contingency_table = pd.crosstab(df['borough'], df['over2h'])

print("Contingency Table (Borough vs. Over 2 Hours):")
print(contingency_table)

chi2, p_value, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(contingency_table)

print(f"Chi-square statistic: {chi2:.4f}")
print(f"P-value: {p_value:.4f}")
print(f"Degrees of freedom: {dof}")
```
There is a statistically significant association between borough and whether a
request takes over 2 hours.

## Data Analysis.

From my testing with geopy I realized that many of the addresses are
non-standard, for example:

* `19 1/2 Pitt Street`
	* This has 1/2 in its name, which geopy will fail to recognize.
* `86th St & Transverse Road`
	* This is an intersection which may fail.
* `2271-89 8th Avenue`
	* This is a range of buildings which will fail.

There were many errors like this, which lead to a lot of missing data which
would cause my analysis of distances to be inconsistent. Fixing all of these
seemingly uncorrelated errors would be tedious, so I changed my approach.

I decided to use OpenCage, which is a geocoder api that is significantly more
powerful than geopy. In order to use OpenCage I needed an api key, although it
was very simple to get one.

In spirit of reproducibility these are the steps:

1. Visit the [OpenCage sign up page](https://opencagedata.com/users/sign_up)
2. Sign up using your email, and answer a few questions.
3. Then you will be taken to a dashboard where you will be presented with an API key.

In order to compile this project just place your api key into the
`OPENCAGE_API_KEY` variable in the code below:

The full line in the code below is: `OPENCAGE_API_KEY = 'YOUR API KEY HERE'`.

OpenCage can catch most of the errors that geopy could not. There was only
a problem with one address, the 103rd precinct with address: `168-02 P.O
Edward Byrne Ave.` in the `nypd_precincts.csv`, only one address error is much
more manageable.

In order to fix this error I simply found the address of the 103rd precinct using
Google: `168-02 91st Ave, Jamaica, NY 11432`, then replaced it within our data,
and used OpenCage like normal.

I also rounded the coordinates to the 5th decimal place in order to match the
noise complaint data.

```{.python}
from opencage.geocoder import OpenCageGeocode
import time

# Set up OpenCage API key (only needs to be set once)
OPENCAGE_API_KEY = 'YOUR API KEY HERE'
geocoder = OpenCageGeocode(OPENCAGE_API_KEY)

# Load and clean data
precinct_df = pd.read_csv('data/nypd_precincts.csv', encoding='latin-1')
clean_precinct_df = precinct_df.dropna(subset=['Address']).copy()

clean_precinct_df.loc[clean_precinct_df['Precinct'].str.contains('103', na=False), 'Address'] = '168-02 91st Ave, Jamaica, NY 11432'

# Geocode
lats, lngs = [], []
for address in clean_precinct_df['Address']:
    try:
        result = geocoder.geocode(address)
        if result and len(result):
            print(address)
            lats.append(result[0]['geometry']['lat'])
            lngs.append(result[0]['geometry']['lng'])
        else:
            print(f"FAILED: {address}")
            lats.append(None)
            lngs.append(None)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"ERROR on {address}: {e}")
        lats.append(None)
        lngs.append(None)

# Add to DataFrame and save
clean_precinct_df['latitude'] = lats
clean_precinct_df['longitude'] = lngs

clean_precinct_df = clean_precinct_df.round({'latitude': 5, 'longitude': 5})

clean_precinct_df.to_csv('data/nypd_precincts_geocoded.csv', index=False)

print("Done")
```

I then load this geocoded precinct data into a variable called `df_p`.

```{python}
df_p = pd.read_csv('data/nypd_precincts_geocoded.csv')
df_p.head()
```

There are many rows that are missing coordinate data in the noise complaint
data set. Many of these rows still contain address information, so we can use
OpenCage to get their coordinates. Although there are still some rows that do
not contain even borough data or address data, we learned this from a previous
cleaning step. I ignore these rows, then round and save to a new feather file.

```{.python}
missing_coords_mask = df['latitude'].isna() & df['longitude'].isna() & df['borough'].notna()

# Create a new DataFrame containing only the rows that meet all conditions
df_to_geocode = df[missing_coords_mask].copy()

# If there are no matching rows, we can stop
if len(df_to_geocode) == 0:
    print("No rows to geocode.")
else:
    # Use the geocoder already initialized above
    lats = []
    lngs = []

    # Iterate over the DataFrame that needs geocoding
    for index, row in df_to_geocode.iterrows():
        address = row['incident_address']
        borough = row['borough'] # We know this is not NaN because of our mask
        
        # Create a full, well-formatted address string
        full_address = f"{address}, {borough}, NY, USA"
        
        print(f"{full_address}")
        
        try:
            result = geocoder.geocode(full_address)
            if result and len(result):
                lats.append(result[0]['geometry']['lat'])
                lngs.append(result[0]['geometry']['lng'])
            else:
                print(f"FAILED {full_address}")
                lats.append(None)
                lngs.append(None)
                
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"ERROR{full_address}: {e}")
            lats.append(None)
            lngs.append(None)
        
        # be respectful to the api!
        time.sleep(1)

    df_to_geocode['latitude'] = lats
    df_to_geocode['longitude'] = lngs

    # Use the index to update the original DataFrame 'df' in place
    df.update(df_to_geocode)

df[['latitude', 'longitude']] = df[['latitude', 'longitude']].round(5)
df.to_feather('data/nypd311w06225noise_by100625_cleaned.arrow')
```

### Getting the distance to closest precinct.

First we read our dataframe that has fixed coordinate data.

```{python}
df = pd.read_feather('data/nypd311w062925noise_by100625_cleaned.arrow')
```

We can use cKDTree to find the nearest precinct using our geocoded precinct
data.

cKDTree is basically a very fast, nearest distance algorithm.

Since our data is so large, and NYC is not a very large area I thought it would
be ok to approximate the coordinates by simply converting latitude and
longitude data to km by multiplying by a constant in order to save computation time.

```{python}
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree
import numpy as np

# Filter out rows with missing coordinates from BOTH dataframes
df_with_coords = df.dropna(subset=['latitude', 'longitude']).copy()
df_p_clean = df_p.dropna(subset=['latitude', 'longitude']).copy()

# Get coordinates
precinct_coords = df_p_clean[['latitude', 'longitude']].values
complaint_coords = df_with_coords[['latitude', 'longitude']].values

# At NYC's latitude (~40.7°), 1° longitude ≈ 85 km, 1° latitude ≈ 111 km
lat_scale = 111.0  # km per degree latitude
lon_scale = 85.0   # km per degree longitude (approximate for NYC)

# Scale coordinates to kilometers
precinct_coords_scaled = precinct_coords.copy()
precinct_coords_scaled[:, 0] *= lat_scale
precinct_coords_scaled[:, 1] *= lon_scale

complaint_coords_scaled = complaint_coords.copy()
complaint_coords_scaled[:, 0] *= lat_scale
complaint_coords_scaled[:, 1] *= lon_scale
```

We can now build the tree, then query it to get our nearest precinct and its
distance. We then apply this back to our noise complaint dataset.

I also made sure to add back in the `over2h` variable in order to continue with
further analysis.

Finally saved that data into a new file.

```{python}
# Build KD-Tree
tree = cKDTree(precinct_coords_scaled)

# Query for nearest neighbor
distances, indices = tree.query(complaint_coords_scaled)

# Add to dataframe
df_with_coords['dist2pp'] = distances
df_with_coords['nearest_precinct'] = df_p_clean.iloc[indices]['Precinct'].values

# Initialize the columns in the original dataframe
df['dist2pp'] = np.nan
df['nearest_precinct'] = None

# Update using loc with the index from df_with_coords
df.loc[df_with_coords.index, 'dist2pp'] = df_with_coords['dist2pp']
df.loc[df_with_coords.index, 'nearest_precinct'] = df_with_coords['nearest_precinct']

print(df['dist2pp'].describe())

# Create response_time and over2h
df['response_time'] = (df['closed_date'] - df['created_date']).dt.total_seconds() / 3600
df['over2h'] = df['response_time'] >= 2

df.to_feather('data/nypd311w062925noise_by100625_with_distances.arrow')

df.head()
```

### Apply Census Data to the dataset.

I decided to use median household income for my analysis, which was obtained
from the US Census website.

```{python}
# Load census data
census_df = pd.read_csv('data/ACSST5Y2023.S1901-Data.csv', header=0, skiprows=[1])
```

### Logistic Regression.

Load our complete data.

```{python}
# Load the data with all features
df = pd.read_feather('data/nypd311w062925noise_by100625_with_distances.arrow')

print(f"Total rows: {len(df)}")
print(f"Columns: {df.columns.tolist()}")
```
Add a lot of predictors to see if they make a good model.

```{python}
# Create time-based features
df['hour'] = df['created_date'].dt.hour
df['day_of_week'] = df['created_date'].dt.dayofweek
df['month'] = df['created_date'].dt.month
df['is_weekend'] = (df['day_of_week'] >= 5).astype(int)
df['is_night'] = ((df['hour'] >= 20) | (df['hour'] < 6)).astype(int)

print(f"Sample of new features:")
print(df[['hour', 'day_of_week', 'is_weekend', 'is_night']].head())
```

Add these feature columns into our data for analysis. And clean the missing
data.

```{python}
# Select features for modeling
feature_cols = ['descriptor', 'borough', 'hour', 'day_of_week', 'month', 
                'is_weekend', 'is_night', 'dist2pp', 'median_household_income']

# Create clean dataset (remove rows with missing values)
df_model = df[feature_cols + ['over2h']].copy()
df_model = df_model.dropna()
```

One hot encode our categorical data to allow our logistic regression to work. 
```{python}
# One-hot encode categorical variables
df_encoded = pd.get_dummies(df_model, columns=['descriptor', 'borough'], drop_first=True)
```

Collect our predictors and use `over2hr` as predicted value, being sure to use
random seed '1234' and split the data 80/20

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Separate features and target
X = df_encoded.drop('over2h', axis=1)
y = df_encoded['over2h']

# Split into train and test (80/20 with seed 1234)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1234, stratify=y
)
```

Scale our numerical fields so that they do not overpower the model. 

```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Scale numerical features
scaler = StandardScaler()
numerical_features = ['hour', 'day_of_week', 'month', 'is_weekend', 
                      'is_night', 'dist2pp', 'median_household_income']

X_train_scaled = X_train.copy()
X_test_scaled = X_test.copy()

X_train_scaled[numerical_features] = scaler.fit_transform(X_train[numerical_features])
X_test_scaled[numerical_features] = scaler.transform(X_test[numerical_features])
```


Build and train the logistic regression model with balanced class weights. From
my testing balanced was the best for my data.

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

logit_model = LogisticRegression(
    C=1.0,
    max_iter=1000,
    random_state=1234,
    solver='lbfgs',
    class_weight='balanced'
)

logit_model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
```

We now test our data and print the results.
```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix, roc_auc_score

# Make predictions on test set
y_test_pred = logit_model.predict(X_test_scaled)
y_test_pred_proba = logit_model.predict_proba(X_test_scaled)[:, 1]

# Evaluate performance
print(classification_report(y_test, y_test_pred))
print(f"\nROC-AUC Score: {roc_auc_score(y_test, y_test_pred_proba):.4f}")

print("\nConfusion Matrix:")
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_test_pred)
print(cm)
```
As you can see my model is not very strong, seeing as the best possible ROC-AUC
is 1, my score is on the lower end, but still better than random guessing which
would be a score of 0.5.

We can also see what factors have the greatest prediction power.

```{python}
feature_importance = pd.DataFrame({
    'feature': X_train_scaled.columns,
    'coefficient': logit_model.coef_[0]
})
feature_importance['abs_coefficient'] = abs(feature_importance['coefficient'])
feature_importance = feature_importance.sort_values('abs_coefficient', ascending=False)

print(feature_importance.head(15).to_string(index=False))
```
### Summary in plain english

From this analysis I have found that it is very difficult to predict police
response times. The most significant feature in my model was being in Brooklyn.
Meaning Brooklyn noise complaints get faster response times on average.

Also another significant finding is that proximity to a police department does
not mean faster response times for your noise complaints.

I believe this is likely because police officers that investigate noise
complaints are usually on patrol, meaning they are not in the police station
when asked to investigate a call.
